description_full: The TJX Companies, Inc., together with its subsidiaries, operates as an off-price apparel and home fashions retailer worldwide. It operates through four segments: Marmaxx, HomeGoods, TJX Canada, and TJX International. The company provides family apparel comprising footwear; accessories, such as beauty and jewelry; home fashion products, including home basics, decorative accessories and giftware, as well as furniture, rugs, lighting, soft home, decorative accessories, tabletop, and cookware; pet and gourmet food; and other merchandise. It also offers home decor, furniture, and seasonal home merchandise. The company sells its products through stores and e-commerce sites. The TJX Companies, Inc. was incorporated in 1962 and is headquartered in Framingham, Massachusetts.
ceo_bio: Mr. Ernie L. Herrman | CEO, President & Director | Age 64 | Compensation: $10.7M (FY2026)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 377K people. Revenue per employee of $160K ranks in the bottom quartile among Consumer Cyclical peers, improving at 7%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $13K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $568 per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 67× revenue per employee (elevated relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags elevated compensation governance risk (7/10).
financial_summary: TJX Companies, Inc. (The) is a large-cap consumer cyclical business with a $148.8B market cap on $60.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +7% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 95% against a 8% cost of capital — a 87-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $4.9B in free cash flow — roughly 8 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.25× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 92× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 2.7% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

E-commerce margin compression and tariff exposure — digital competition erodes pricing power while trade policy reshuffles supply-chain cost structures overnight.
Brand relevance decay — shifting consumer preferences and social-media-driven trends can strand inventory and invalidate positioning faster than product cycles can adapt.

sect: Its 12% operating margin is roughly in line with the Consumer Cyclical median (8%).
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.46x).
It accounts for 1.2% of sector revenue and 1.7% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+4.1% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 20% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 23% and a beta of 0.69, it is more defensive than the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $991.8M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 43% in the 2020 crash, 28% in the 2022 bear market and 50% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $123 (margin of safety -10%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 13%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $92.16 to $168 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/E 25.1 vs 19.3, EV/EBITDA 18.1 vs 11.2 and P/FCF 30.3 vs 16.5 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 27% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.3% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.5% (vs the 8% bar).
The 19 covering analysts target $171 on average, 27% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 95% clears the cost of capital of 8.1% by 87pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.44).
It converts 8% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.25x.
ROE of 54% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (3.5x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.4% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $3.4B (2% of market cap).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 6.5% over 3 years and 6.2% over 10 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 13%).
At current returns, reinvesting 10% of profits supports about 9.8% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Capex runs 1.6x depreciation (3.2% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 7.0% on average.
Analysts expect 10.2% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.2%), and institutions hold 95%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (7 sales, net $25.9M sold).
It returns 2.7% a year to shareholders (1.5% in buybacks and 1.4% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 1.6% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 38 consecutive years, raising it 45.9% a year over the last five.
people: With about 377,000 employees, each generates about $160K of revenue, 0.4x the Consumer Cyclical median, and productivity has risen 6.6% a year.
That works out to $13K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $10.7M (67x revenue per employee).
